intro: There are no wrong answers. Honest answers get you better advice. If you're not sure, tap "Not sure" and we'll add it to your list to check.

prompts.title: Do you need a code from your phone to log in?
prompts.why: This is called two-step login. Even if someone steals a password, they can't get in without the code from your phone. Email matters most because password resets go there, and your money and load tools are what criminals want.

rows.question: Q1
rows.label: Company email

rows.question: Q2
rows.label: Banking, accounting, and other business websites

labelBySector.carrier: Banking, accounting, load boards, and fleet or TMS portals
labelBySector.broker: Banking, accounting, load boards, and TMS portals
labelBySector.farm: Banking, accounting, and co-op or grain marketing accounts

prompts.title: Accounts and passwords
prompts.why: Shared logins hide who did what and can't be switched off for one person. Old accounts of people who left are an easy way in. Reused passwords turn one website's breach into many. Admin rights on everyday accounts let one bad click take over a computer.

rows.question: Q3
rows.label: Does everyone have their own login, with no shared accounts or shared tablets?

rows.question: Q4
rows.label: When someone leaves, how soon is their access removed?

options.label: It can take longer or get missed

rows.question: Q5
rows.label: How do people keep track of passwords?

options.label: Memory, paper, or the same password everywhere

rows.question: Q6
rows.label: Who has admin rights to install software on work computers?

options.label: Only one or two trusted people

prompts.title: Payments and load changes
prompts.why: Most payment fraud starts with an email saying "we changed banks." Calling a number you already trust, not the one in the email, stops it. A second person approving big payments catches rushed or unusual requests. The same trick works on loads: a fake "new delivery address" email that one person acts on alone.

rows.question: Q7
rows.label: Before changing a supplier's or carrier's bank details, do you call them at a number you already had on file?

rows.question: Q8
rows.label: Do large payments need a second person to approve them?

rows.question: Q26
rows.label: If someone emails to change a pickup or delivery address, can one person make the change on their own?

labelBySector.carrier: If a broker or shipper emails to change a pickup or delivery address, can one dispatcher make the change on their own?
labelBySector.broker: If a shipper or carrier emails to change a pickup or delivery address, can one person make the change on their own?

options.label: No, we call back on a known number and a second person OKs it
We call back, but one person can still change it
Yes, one person can change it from the email

prompts.title: Email
prompts.why: Most attacks start with an email. Short training helps people pause before clicking. An "External" label shows when a message claiming to be from your boss came from outside. DMARC stops strangers sending email that looks like it came from your company, such as fake invoices to your customers.

rows.question: Q9
rows.label: Has your team had any training on spotting fake emails in the past year?

rows.question: Q10
rows.label: Do emails from outside the company show a warning label?

rows.question: Q11
rows.label: Is your email domain protected against spoofing (DMARC)?
rows.labelBasic: Is your company email set up so strangers can't send fake emails that look like they came from you? (The email check can answer this.)

prompts.title: Computers, phones, and tablets
prompts.why: Attackers use known holes in old software, and automatic updates close them. Built-in antivirus like Microsoft Defender blocks most common malware, but only if it's on. A lost phone or truck tablet can hold email and saved passwords.

rows.question: Q12
rows.label: Do computers install security updates automatically?

rows.question: Q13
rows.label: Is antivirus (like Microsoft Defender) turned on?

rows.question: Q16
rows.label: Are work phones and tablets locked with a PIN, and can you wipe them remotely if they're lost?

options.label: Only one of these, or only some devices

rows.na: We don't use phones or tablets for work

prompts.title: How are your files and business data backed up?
prompts.why: Backups let you recover from ransomware or a dead hard drive without paying anyone. Ransomware hunts for backups it can reach, so the copy that saves you is one that's offline or separate, and that you've actually restored from.

options.label: Now and then, when someone remembers
Regularly, but only one copy, and we've never tried restoring it
Regularly, plus either an offline copy or a restore we've tested (not both)
Regularly, with an offline or separate copy we've restored from

prompts.title: Connecting from outside the office
prompts.why: Remote desktop left open to the internet is one of the top ways ransomware gangs get in. A secure connection that also needs a phone code closes that door.

rows.question: Q17
rows.label: When people connect to office computers from home or on the road, how do they do it?

options.label: A secure connection that needs a phone code
A secure connection, but no phone code
Remote desktop or a remote tool with just a password

rows.na: Nobody connects from outside the office

prompts.title: Equipment, routers, and Wi-Fi
prompts.why: Always-on vendor remote access is an open door to your equipment. A separate network keeps an infected office computer away from refrigeration or sensors. Factory passwords like "admin" are published online. Visitors' and drivers' phones shouldn't share a network with your business computers.

rows.question: Q18
rows.label: Is vendor remote access to your equipment (TeamViewer, AnyDesk) switched off when it's not being used?

rows.question: Q19
rows.label: Is your connected equipment on a separate network from office computers?
rows.labelBasic: Are fridges, sensors, and cameras on a separate Wi-Fi or network from your office computers?

rows.question: Q20
rows.label: Have the default passwords been changed on routers, cameras, and equipment?

rows.question: Q21
rows.label: Is guest or driver Wi-Fi separate from your business network?

prompts.title: Vendors and IT providers
prompts.why: You can't protect a door you don't know about, so keep a list of who can get into your systems. If a vendor is hacked and doesn't tell you, attackers can use that access for weeks.

rows.question: Q22
rows.label: Do you keep a list of every vendor or IT provider that can access your systems?

options.label: Yes, and it's up to date

rows.question: Q23
rows.label: Do your contracts require vendors to tell you if they're hacked?

prompts.title: If something goes wrong
prompts.why: These don't stop an attack, but they make every attack less damaging. A one-page plan saves hours of panic. Cyber insurance helps pay for recovery and often includes expert help on the day.

rows.question: Q24
rows.label: Do you have a written list of who to call and what to do if you get hacked?

rows.question: Q25
rows.label: Do you have cyber insurance?

options.label: Some cover, but not sure it includes cyber attacks
